rationale: Round 1 built and ran correctly, so this round pushes obfuscation harder while respecting the program's nature: a tiny (810-byte, 2-function) floating-point throughput kernel where every transformed instruction sits in the hot loop. SUB gets the highest security and diversity weights because arithmetic substitution directly obscures the FP computations that define this benchmark at near-zero cost, and SPLIT is similarly cheap structural diversity. IBR is favored moderately to obscure the loop control flow. FLA is kept at a middling security weight with elevated runtime/size costs since control-flow flattening overhead is paid per iteration; BCF is actively dampened (high RuntimeCost/SizeCost weights, low SecurityGain) because bogus-condition evaluation in a tight FP loop is the worst overhead-to-benefit trade here. ICALL stays mild given the near-total absence of call sites, and IGV is effectively disabled since the program has almost no global variable indirection to hide. Overall the table biases toward cheap, correctness-safe transformations that maximize static analysis confusion of the numeric core while keeping runtime growth acceptable.
